title: India's cyber agency sets four risk tiers for auditing AI systems, including agents
excerpt: India's CERT-In published AI security auditing guidelines on 4 November 2026. Higher-risk systems, including some AI agents, face independent audits and must stay stoppable and reversible.

sources.title: CERT-In: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0 (4 November 2026)
The 420.in: CERT-In Issues AI Security Audit Guidelines, Sets Four Risk Categories
Risk Management Association of India: CERT-In Releases AI Security Auditing Guidelines 2026

body_html:
India's national cyber security agency, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), published its first AI Security Auditing Guidelines on 4 November 2026. The 107-page document sets out how AI systems used in India should be checked for security, privacy, fairness, transparency and human oversight, and how often.

The guidelines cover organisations that operate AI systems in India or process the data of Indian citizens: government bodies, state-owned companies, critical infrastructure operators, regulated firms, private companies, small businesses, start-ups, and AI developers and service providers. AI used only for research or for purely personal use is outside the mandatory scope. Systems built in-house, bought, accessed through an online interface or downloaded as open source are all covered, including AI agents and AI that controls physical equipment.

Four risk tiers

Each AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight factors: how severe the harm could be, how much it acts on its own, how sensitive its data is, how widely it is used, whether its effects can be reversed, how critical its sector is, how exposed it is to attack, and how hard it is to audit. The total places it in one of four tiers: Low, Moderate, High or Critical.

  • Low: assistive tools with limited autonomy and impact. A yearly review or self-assessment, covering governance and security.
  • Moderate and High: systems that shape business processes or consequential decisions. All nine audit areas apply, and independent audits by CERT-In-approved ("empanelled") audit organisations come in as the risk rises.
  • Critical: systems in critical infrastructure, national security or safety-critical uses. Independent audits plus continuous monitoring and reassessment after significant events.

Auditors must check the tier themselves and use the higher one if they disagree with the organisation. A system is pushed up a tier if it takes consequential actions on its own, holds privileged access, or cannot be safely interrupted or rolled back.

What it asks of AI agents

For AI that acts rather than only answers, the guidelines ask for human approval before consequential actions, a way for people to override or intervene, and regular tests that this oversight actually works. Oversight must allow the system to be constrained, changed or shut down. Organisations are also asked to keep tamper-protected logs of decisions and overrides, to be able to roll back changes or fall back to a safe mode, and to give connectors and service accounts only the access they need.

The nine audit areas also include data quality and privacy, bias and fairness, explainability, monitoring for drift, and checks on third-party models and suppliers. A lack of access to a supplier's model is not treated as proof that it is safe.

The guidelines also set a limit on the auditors' own use of AI. In CERT-In's words: "AI-generated outputs shall not replace sufficient and appropriate evidence or the auditor's independent judgement."

What is not yet clear

The document mostly uses "shall" language, but The 420.in notes that it does not by itself create a standalone AI law. Its six-hour deadline for reporting qualifying AI security incidents and its 180-day log retention build on existing CERT-In directions from 2022. How CERT-In will check compliance, and how small firms will bear the cost of audits, has not been set out. Commentators at the Risk Management Association of India also say they could not yet review every clause in detail.

Why it matters for staying in charge

The guidelines tie the depth of checking to what a system can do and whether its effects can be undone. That matches several Humasure Directives: a person must be able to stop the system (D1 Always stoppable), an agent should act only within agreed limits (D2 Bounded autonomy), security has to be kept up over time (D6 Secure and supported), and someone must be answerable for the result (D9 Accountable).

Wherever you live, you can ask the same things of any AI product: what risk level its maker assigned it, who checked that, and how you stop it. See our Questions to ask and Security pages.
